name: Braces / orthodontics for jaw shape

lead: Braces and other orthodontic appliances align teeth and bite, and in growing patients can guide jaws. People interested in appearance discuss them for a better profile and smile, often alongside jaw surgery.

Appliances apply sustained force to move teeth through bone, and palatal expanders and headgear can alter jaw alignment or airflow. Clinicians learned that perfect occlusion alone does not ensure good facial appearance. Severe jaw discrepancies may need surgery combined with orthodontics. Registered trials mostly address alignment speed, sleep and airway rather than facial attractiveness.

paras: Treatment is planned by an orthodontist and runs for months to years, with retainers afterward. For skeletal problems it is paired with jaw surgery before and after the operation.
Decalcification and decay with poor hygiene are described, and relapse is frequent, so retainers are often recommended. Facial-aesthetic outcomes are less studied than dental ones.

angle.text: A better bite, straighter teeth and a more balanced profile and smile. Appliances align teeth and guide jaw position, and combined with jaw surgery they can change the profile more. Studies focus on dental outcomes more than facial looks.

lead: Orthodontics is the dental specialty that diagnoses, prevents and corrects misaligned teeth, jaws and bite patterns, and in growing patients can also guide facial growth; braces are its best-known tool [1]. People use orthodontic treatment to look better in two ways. Straightening and aligning the teeth changes the smile directly, and correcting the bite changes how the upper and lower teeth meet, which affects how the lips rest and how the lower face and profile look from the side, especially when braces are combined with jaw surgery [1][2][3].

In looksmaxxing communities braces are discussed as one of the more accessible ways to work on the lower third of the face. Members of looksmax.org describe bite-correcting elastics, palatal expanders and extraction or non-extraction plans, compare appliance types and timing, and argue over whether treatment improves or recesses the profile [4][5][6][7]. One widely repeated thread argues that braces are an inexpensive route to better jaw projection for people who are eligible, while others describe regret after extractions or retraction of the front teeth [4][6].

Orthodontists distinguish between moving teeth, which braces do reliably, and changing the position of the jaws, which in most adults requires surgery and in children can sometimes be influenced with growth-modifying appliances [1][3][8]. Published and registered human research in the area mostly measures alignment speed, finished-case quality, speech, sleep and airway outcomes, while systematic reviews of extraction and non-extraction treatment report changes in lip position relative to the profile [9][10][11][12][13].

The entry covers the main appliance types, how treatment is planned for bite and profile, the history from Fauchard and Angle to modern straight-wire systems, what research and clinicians report, the risks, and how the topic circulates in appearance forums.

paras: Orthodontic treatment moves teeth through bone with sustained, light forces and, in children and teenagers, can steer jaw growth. Treatment usually begins before adulthood, when the jaws are still developing, and may take several months to a few years [1]. Abnormal alignment of teeth and jaws is common, with worldwide malocclusion prevalence reported as high as 56% [1].

Braces work by keeping constant pressure on a tooth. The ligament that holds the tooth is compressed on one side and stretched on the other, and bone is then remodelled around the tooth in its new position, which is why movement is slow and appointments are spaced out [2]. The four traditional components are brackets, bonding material, an archwire and ligature elastics, with springs or rubber bands added to apply force in specific directions; modern wires are often nickel-titanium, which stays flexible and applies light force [2].

Appliances fall into two groups. Removable appliances, such as clear retainers, Hawley retainers, palatal expanders and clear aligners including Invisalign, can be taken out by the patient. Fixed appliances are bonded to the teeth and stay in place during treatment; nearly all modern fixed braces are variations on the edgewise system introduced by Edward Angle in 1928 [1]. Headgear, functional appliances and reverse-pull facemasks are used in growing patients to influence jaw relationships [1].

Orthodontists describe bite problems with Edward Angle's classes, based on how the first molars meet. In Class I the molar relationship is normal but teeth may be crowded or spaced. In Class II the upper molar sits forward of its normal position relative to the lower one, which is often seen with protruded upper front teeth and a large overjet or with a small lower jaw. In Class III the upper molar sits behind its normal position, often reflecting a large lower jaw or short upper jaw and appearing as an underbite [8].

Overbite is the vertical overlap of the upper and lower front teeth and overjet is the horizontal distance between them. Increased vertical facial growth tends to go with a long face and open bite, decreased vertical growth with a short face and deep bite, and under- or overgrowth of the lower jaw with Class II and Class III patterns [8]. Critics of Angle's system note that it is two-dimensional and describes the bite without addressing causes or facial proportions [8].

Wikipedia reports that about 30% of people have a malocclusion considered severe enough to benefit from orthodontics, and that jaw surgery for severe cases is needed in about 5% of the general population [8]. Poorly aligned teeth can significantly affect self-esteem, and skeletal malocclusions can distort facial shape [8].

Aligning crowded, rotated or gapped teeth changes the visible smile line. Correcting an overbite or overjet changes where the upper and lower front teeth sit relative to each other, which affects how the lips rest and how the chin appears in side view [1]. Extraction of teeth, usually premolars, occurs in about half of treatments and is used to relieve crowding or retract protruding front teeth [1].

Braces are used for appearance even where treatment is not medically necessary, and cosmetic use is described as more common in countries with wealthier economies [2]. Colourful ligatures allow patients to personalise the look, and clear and lingual appliances were developed for people who do not want visible metal [2].

Where the jaws themselves are mismatched, orthodontists coordinate with oral and maxillofacial surgeons. In that pathway, braces move the teeth into positions that will fit together after the bones are repositioned, and further orthodontic work after surgery finalises the bite [1][3]. Posters on looksmax.org discuss this combined route as an option for larger discrepancies [4].

Beyond appearance, orthodontics addresses chewing function, speech and tooth protection. An overjet over 3 mm is linked to roughly double the risk of front-tooth trauma [8]. Registered studies have followed speech in patients with dentofacial deformities before and after treatment [10], and others have looked at functional appliances and palatal expansion in children with sleep-disordered breathing [11][14][15]. Wikipedia notes that conclusive scientific evidence for health benefits of orthodontic treatment is limited, while patients who complete treatment report higher quality of life than those still in treatment [1].

Traditional metal braces use stainless steel brackets with elastic ties and are the most common type; self-ligating braces replace the ties with a built-in clip and are described as possibly reducing treatment time, pain and the number of adjustments. Gold-plated and titanium versions exist for patients with nickel allergy or aesthetic preferences, and lingual braces are bonded behind the teeth so they are not visible from the front [2].

Lawrence Andrews' straight-wire (pre-adjusted edgewise) system of 1976 built the bracket prescription into the appliance so that wires need minimal bending [1]. Customised systems that use 3-D imaging, planning software and robot-bent wires are described as aiming for faster and more efficient treatment [2].

Clear aligners are a series of removable trays that move teeth progressively. Wikipedia notes that they are generally not used for complex cases involving extractions, jaw surgery or palate expansion [2]. A randomised trial of 66 adults compared Invisalign aligners with SmartForce features and attachments (32 patients) against traditional fixed appliances (34 patients) on finished-case quality, with median ages of about 26 in both groups [12].

Palatal expansion widens the upper jaw so the upper and lower teeth fit together. It is most common between ages 8 and 18; rapid expanders use a central screw turned daily and typically stay in place for three to six months while bone fills the gap, followed by a retainer [16]. Treatment is believed to work best before or during the growth spurt, because after puberty the two halves of the palate fuse and expansion produces more dental than skeletal change; mini-implant-assisted expanders (MARPE) are used in young adults, and surgically assisted expansion for others [16]. Reported side effects include speech changes, headaches, a gap between the upper front teeth, and a loss of one-third to one-half of the expansion before stabilisation [16].

Headgear is used mainly for Class II overbites and is typically worn 12 to 22 hours a day for 12 to 18 months, sometimes only at night, while functional appliances such as the twin block are used in growing patients with Class II patterns [2][8]. For Class III, growth-modification appliances such as the chin cap are described as often relapsing during puberty, with surgery used for larger discrepancies [8].

Retainers follow active treatment: clear (Essix, Zendura, Vivera) or Hawley removable types, or a wire bonded behind the front teeth [1][2]. Without retainers, teeth may drift back toward their original positions, and clear plates are often worn full time for about six months afterwards [2].

Orthodontics reliably moves teeth; the more contested question in appearance communities is how much it changes skeletal profile. Wikipedia reports that more than half of treated patients show some return toward original tooth positions within ten years, and most receive retainers; the usual guidance is full-time wear for about six months and then night-time wear for many years [1].

Clinicians distinguish dental changes (tooth position) from skeletal ones (jaw position). Functional appliances and expanders are applied during growth, whereas adults with substantial skeletal discrepancies are typically referred for orthognathic surgery [1][3]. Registered paediatric studies measure outcomes such as airway size and sleep quality after functional treatment [11][14][15].

sections.h: Profile changes and the extraction debate
paras: Extraction of premolars to relieve crowding or retract protruding front teeth is the most discussed route in appearance forums, because pulling the front teeth back can change lip position. Tweed in the United States and Begg in Australia reintroduced extraction in the 1940s and 1950s specifically to improve facial balance and stability, after Angle's opposition to it [1].

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis in The Angle Orthodontist by Elias, Sivamurthy and Bearn pooled 30 studies, 29 of them retrospective and one randomised, comparing four-first-premolar extraction with non-extraction treatment. For the profile, the authors counted studies and reported that extraction produced retraction of both lips relative to the E-plane (a reference line from the nose tip to the chin tip), with individual studies disagreeing on the upper and lower lip and the evidence rated very low certainty on the GRADE scale [13].

The authors also noted that ethnic differences between study populations limited pooling [13]. Orthodontists generally describe profile outcomes as depending on the type of malocclusion, which teeth are removed and how far the front teeth are retracted, and the extraction question remains one that clinicians debate [1][13].

Orthognathic surgery realigns the jaws and lower face and is used for skeletal and bite problems, airway issues including sleep apnoea, and facial asymmetry or proportion concerns [3]. Surgeons (oral and maxillofacial or plastic) work with orthodontists, and patients usually wear braces before and after surgery, followed by retainers; presurgical orthodontics with metal braces can last up to a year, while newer approaches include surgery-first and clear aligners [3].

Common procedures include Le Fort I for the upper jaw, the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO), developed by Hugo Obwegeser, for the lower jaw, and genioplasty for the chin [3]. Wikipedia reports that the surgery usually produces a noticeable change in the face, that planning software can predict the post-operative appearance, and that initial healing takes two to six weeks, with bone remodelling taking a further two to four months [3]. Reported risks include swelling, infection (up to 7% in some reports) and facial numbness from nerve injury that usually recovers within three months [3].

Fixed appliances make cleaning more difficult. Plaque is almost unavoidable, gingivitis and gum recession occur in many patients, and decalcification (white-spot lesions) and decay are described risks, which is why fixed braces are not preferred for patients with poor oral hygiene [1][2]. A randomised trial examined enamel demineralisation prevention during treatment with non-removable appliances [17], and a trial in fixed-appliance patients tested different tooth-brushing explanations to improve plaque control [18].

Pain after fitting or adjustment is very common, and a 2017 Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found moderate-quality evidence that analgesics reduce orthodontic pain [2]. Most treatment causes some degree of root resorption, which is rarely severe enough to cause real damage [2].
Relapse after treatment is common, and compliance with elastics, retainers and check-ups is described by treated patients as decisive for the result [1][4][2].

Evidence from Greek and Etruscan materials suggests attempts to straighten teeth date to about 1000 BC [1]. Wikipedia's dental braces article describes Hippocrates and Aristotle considering ways to straighten teeth around 400 to 300 BC [2]. Pierre Fauchard, often credited with founding modern orthodontics, published a book on straightening teeth in 1728 and used a horseshoe-shaped iron device called the Bandeau to expand the palate; in 1754 Louis Bourdet refined it and was the first on record to recommend extracting premolars to relieve crowding [2]. Christophe Delabarre introduced the wire crib in 1819 [2].

Modern orthodontics took shape in the mid-1800s. Norman Kingsley (1829-1913) published Oral Deformities and used extraoral force to correct protruding teeth, and Edward Angle (1855-1930), regarded as the father of modern orthodontics, created the classification of malocclusion still used today [1][2]. Angle introduced a sequence of appliances (E-arch in 1907, pin and tube, ribbon arch and the edgewise appliance in 1928) [1].

Angle opposed tooth extraction, but Charles Tweed and Raymond Begg reintroduced it in the 1940s and 1950s to improve facial balance and stability of results; Begg developed his light-wire appliance in the late 1930s [1]. After World War II, cephalometric X-rays showed that many Class II and Class III problems come from jaw relationships rather than teeth alone [1]. Bonded brackets replaced wrapped metal bands by the mid-1970s, the same decade Andrews introduced the straight-wire appliance [1]. Nickel-titanium wire, developed from Nitinol (first made at the Naval Ordnance Laboratory in 1959), was applied to whole treatments by George Andreasen in 1979, reducing visits and discomfort [2].

Threads on looksmax.org ask whether braces improve or recess the face. One poster who wore braces for 2 years and 4 months from age 16, with elastics to correct a recessed jaw and significant overbite, argued that braces are a relatively inexpensive route to better jaw projection and that results depend on following the orthodontist's instructions, including elastics and retainers [4]. Another thread starter asked whether braces with rubber bands recess the face, saying friends had told him braces make people look better and that he only wanted to correct an overbite [7].

Others report worry after seeing short-form videos claiming braces cause recession and restrict maxilla and mandible growth [5], and at least one thread describes a user who felt their face had receded after treatment [6]. Adult treatment is described by posters as slower and giving smaller changes than treatment in teenagers [4]. Palatal expansion in adults, the question of extractions, and combining braces with surgery are recurring subjects, and wider appearance culture also discusses non-orthodontic jaw practices such as mewing, which orthodontic bodies have commented on separately.

Muscle-building forums also mention practicalities: a T Nation member described starting Invisalign and expecting it to make frequent calorie-dense snacking harder, since the trays must come out for eating [19].

Registered and published studies in this area mostly measure alignment, speech, sleep and airway outcomes. A trial of ways to accelerate alignment of crowded lower front teeth enrolled 38 patients (completed) [9]. A study of speech in patients with dentofacial deformities before and after orthodontic or surgical treatment targets 180 participants [10]. Trials in children include a functional-appliance study of sleep quality and upper airway in 46 patients with mandibular retrognathia [11], a study of sleep, airway and occlusion in 69 children with large overjet [14], and an earlier study of pharyngeal size in 40 patients with obstructive tonsils under orthodontic treatment [20]. A trial of maxillary expansion in paediatric sleep apnoea enrolled 14 participants [15]. A mandibular repositioning appliance for adult snoring and sleep apnoea was studied in 96 patients [21].

A randomised trial of 66 patients compared Invisalign with fixed appliances on finished-case quality [12]. Another randomised trial looked at enamel demineralisation with non-removable appliances [17]. The 2024 meta-analysis of extraction versus non-extraction treatment reported lip-position changes in 30 mostly retrospective studies [13]. None of the trials above primarily rates facial attractiveness.

lore.intro: Braces are among the most discussed hardmaxxing-adjacent topics on looksmax.org, mainly around whether orthodontics improves or recesses the profile, whether adults gain much, and how to combine braces with surgery [4][5][6][7].
